case_name: Welcome Hotel and Others v State of Andhra Pradesh and Others
facts: The Welcome Hotel and Others v State of Andhra Pradesh and Others case was heard by the Supreme Court of India on August 22, 1983.
The case involved a group of petitions filed by hoteliers in Andhra Pradesh challenging the Andhra Pradesh Catering Establishments (Fixation and Display of Prices of Foodstuffs) Order, 1978.

The order required catering establishments to display prices of all foodstuffs served and fixed maximum prices for certain items, including idli, vada, upma, sada dosa, puree, coffee, tea, and a rice plate.
The petitioners argued that the order was unconstitutional and sought an ex-parte stay on its implementation.
The State Government had issued a clarificatory notification in October 1978 and modified the schedule of prices by an Amending Order dated December 11, 1980.

In January 1981, the Minister of Civil Supplies called a meeting with hoteliers to discuss price reductions, and an undertaking was signed by the hoteliers agreeing to reduce prices for certain items.
The petitioners obtained an ex-parte stay on the order's implementation in January 1981, but this was later lifted.
issues: Whether Art. 32 of the Constitution lends its assistance to petitioners in this group of petitions so that the poor in Andhra Pradesh can be successfully deprived of their staple simple breakfast?
Whether the State Government has the power to issue price control measures in respect of cooked food under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955?
petitioner_arguments: The petitioners argued that the order was unconstitutional and sought an ex-parte stay on its implementation.

They submitted that the Court should give a direction to the State Government to re-examine the prices of inputs and overhead charges so as to arrive at such maximum price of the scheduled commodities as to ensure a reasonable return on the investment which would render the restriction on the fundamental right to carry on trade, reasonable and satisfy Art. 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution.

They also submitted that there are certain directions in the 1978 and 1981 orders which are impossible of compliance and, therefore, the petitioners should be heard before they are compelled to implement the conditions.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that the order was constitutional and necessary for the control of essential commodities.
They submitted that the power to fix prices of essential commodities is implicit in the power conferred by Sec. 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.

They also submitted that the expression 'foodstuffs' includes cooked food and that the State Government has the power to issue price control measures in respect of cooked food under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
court_reasoning: The Court held that the order was constitutional and necessary for the control of essential commodities.
It rejected the petitioners' submissions that the order was unconstitutional and that the State Government should re-examine the prices of inputs and overhead charges.
It also rejected the petitioners' submission that certain directions in the 1978 and 1981 orders were impossible of compliance.

The Court held that the expression 'foodstuffs' includes cooked food and that the State Government has the power to issue price control measures in respect of cooked food under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
holding: The Court dismissed the petitions filed by the hoteliers and upheld the Andhra Pradesh Catering Establishments (Fixation and Display of Prices of Foodstuffs) Order, 1978.
It held that the order was constitutional and necessary for the control of essential commodities.

It also held that the expression 'foodstuffs' includes cooked food and that the State Government has the power to issue price control measures in respect of cooked food under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
